source: Anatomy: OpenKBP patient pt_14 (Babier et al., Med Phys 2021), AP projection of the CT volume. The radiographic effects are simulated.

items.label: Megavoltage beam
items.cap: A 6 MV beam gives images with little Z-dependence, so bone is distinguished from soft tissue only by its density. The bone contrast is far smaller than at kilovoltage energy, where the photoelectric effect adds a strong Z-dependence. Both images use the same window in water thickness, so the soft tissue looks the same and only the bone differs.
items.facts: replacing 2 cm of water by 2 cm of bone changes −ln(I) by 0.95 at kV and 0.085 at MV, a factor of 11. With the same soft-tissue window, the bone region differs from the soft-tissue region by 12% of the display range at kV and 8% at MV

items.label: Exposure 1
items.cap: Photon counting noise. The standard deviation of the signal in a uniform region rises as the exposure falls, as 1 / √(exposure), and the grain hides the weak contrast.

items.label: Scatter, no grid
items.cap: Photons that scatter in the patient reach the detector along the wrong path. They add a smooth background that carries no information, so the contrast falls and the image looks flat.
items.facts: the contrast between the bone and soft-tissue regions falls to 0.15 of its primary-only value (scatter-to-primary ratio 2.0)

items.label: Scatter, with grid
items.cap: The fins of the grid stop most of the scattered photons and pass most of the primary photons. The contrast recovers, at the cost of a higher exposure to make up for the primary photons that the grid also absorbs.
items.facts: the contrast recovers to 0.41 of its primary-only value (scatter-to-primary ratio 0.43), and the exposure must rise 3.0 times (the Bucky factor)
